# Why?

## The Problem

**After every race, teams need answers — fast.**

- Which strategy worked? Which didn't?
- Where on track did we lose time?
- How did tyre degradation affect pace?
- How did our drivers compare to the competition?

. . .

**Today's reality:** Engineers juggle raw CSV exports, separate timing screens, and static broadcast graphics, stitching together a picture manually.

## What We Built

A **single interactive dashboard** that brings together:

- Race strategy overview (all 20 drivers)
- Lap time progression with degradation trendlines
- High-frequency telemetry comparison (driver vs. driver)
- Track map coloured by speed, throttle, brake, or gear

. . .

All powered by **one click** select a season and Grand Prix, and the dashboard loads everything.

# Data Source

## FastF1 The Data Behind F1

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What is it?**

Open-source Python library (MIT licence) that wraps the official F1 timing data APIs.

**What does it provide?**

- Lap-by-lap timing for all 20 drivers
- Tyre compound and stint information
- High-frequency car telemetry (~240 Hz)
- GPS track coordinates (X, Y, Z)
- Race results and classifications
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Data scale per race:**

| Level | Observations |
|---|---|
| Laps | ~1,000+ |
| Telemetry | ~100,000+ |
| Results | 20 |

**Key features:** 15+ variables mix of numerical (speed, throttle, lap time) and categorical (compound, driver, team)
:::
::::


# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Data Quality Missing Values

```{python}
#| label: fig-eda-missing
#| fig-cap: "Missing value fractions in the laps dataset (2025 Bahrain GP)."
#| echo: false
laps_full = session.laps.copy()
for col in ["LapTime", "Sector1Time", "Sector2Time", "Sector3Time"]:
    if col in laps_full.columns:
        laps_full[f"{col}Sec"] = laps_full[col].dt.total_seconds()

analysis_cols = [
    "LapTimeSec", "Sector1TimeSec", "Sector2TimeSec", "Sector3TimeSec",
    "SpeedFL", "SpeedST", "TyreLife", "Position", "Compound"
]
available_cols = [c for c in analysis_cols if c in laps_full.columns]
missing_frac = laps_full[available_cols].isnull().mean().sort_values(ascending=False)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
colors = ["#e8002d" if v > 0.05 else "#4C78A8" for v in missing_frac.values]
missing_frac.plot.barh(ax=ax, color=colors)
ax.set_xlabel("Fraction missing")
ax.axvline(x=0.05, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, label="5% threshold")
ax.legend(facecolor="#0e1117", edgecolor="#333")
ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Implication:** `.dropna(subset=["LapTime"])` removes in-laps and out-laps these are genuinely incomplete, not errors.


## Correlations Telemetry Channels

```{python}
#| label: fig-eda-corr
#| fig-cap: "Spearman correlation between telemetry variables."
#| echo: false
import seaborn as sns

fastest_lap = session.laps.pick_fastest()
tel = fastest_lap.get_telemetry()

tel_numeric = tel[["Speed", "Throttle", "Brake", "nGear", "RPM"]].copy()
tel_numeric["Brake"] = tel_numeric["Brake"].astype(float)
tel_corr = tel_numeric.corr(method="spearman")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
sns.heatmap(tel_corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="RdBu_r", center=0,
            square=True, ax=ax, linewidths=0.5,
            cbar_kws={"shrink": 0.8})
ax.set_title("Spearman Correlation", color="white", fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Speed-Throttle and Speed-Gear strongly correlated. 


# The Dashboard

## Home Page Overview at a Glance

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**KPI Cards:**

- Finishing position per Ferrari driver
- Grid position delta (gained/lost)
- Best lap time
- Total points scored

**Strategy Thumbnail:**

- Compact stint chart for quick context
- Links naturally to the detailed Strategy page
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why these elements?**

- Addresses Giulia's need for an **entry point** — not raw data
- Gives Marco the **executive summary** before diving deeper
- KPI cards provide instant orientation: "How did Ferrari do?"
:::
::::

## Strategy Page Who Did What?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Position Chart** (line chart)

- All 20 drivers, Ferrari highlighted in red
- Y-axis inverted (P1 at top)
- Hover reveals exact position per lap

**Stint Chart** (horizontal stacked bar)

- Colour = tyre compound (red/yellow/white)
- Ferrari bordered in red
- Ordered by finishing position
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why these charts?**

- **Position chart:** Bump chart is the standard for position changes over time — immediately shows overtakes and strategy effects
- **Stint chart:** Horizontal bars map intuitively to the time axis of a race; compound colours are F1 conventions that need no legend explanation
- Both address Marco's need to *"compare competitor strategies"*
:::
::::

## Lap Times Page Degradation Analysis

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Line chart** with:

- Lap time per lap, colour-coded by compound
- Dashed **trendlines** per stint (linear regression)
- PIT markers at stop boundaries
- Optional competitor overlay (grey)

**Filters:**

- Stint selector (multiselect)
- Hide SC / outlier laps toggle (>107% median)
- Competitor comparison dropdown
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why a line chart?**

- Lap times are a **time series** line charts show trends naturally
- Per-stint trendlines make **degradation rate** quantifiable at a glance
- EDA confirmed the tyre life vs. lap time relationship
- Outlier filtering prevents SC laps from distorting the y-axis scale
- Competitor overlay enables **relative** performance comparison
:::
::::

## Telemetry Page Driver vs. Driver

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**3-row subplot layout:**

1. Speed (km/h) over distance
2. Throttle (%) over distance
3. Brake (on/off) over distance

- **Shared x-axis** (distance in meters)
- Driver A in red, Driver B in blue
- Defaults to fastest lap per driver
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why this layout?**

- **Subplots with shared x-axis** let the eye move vertically to link cause and effect: *"Driver A brakes later, carries more speed, higher throttle on exit"*
- Distance (not time) as x-axis ensures spatial alignment on track
- Red vs. blue is the most accessible colour contrast
- This is the **established format** in motorsport telemetry analysis Marco recognises it instantly
:::
::::

## Track Map Where on Track?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Circuit outline** from GPS coordinates (X, Y), coloured by:

- Speed (RdYlGn colorscale)
- Throttle (RdYlGn)
- Brake (RdYlGn reversed)
- Gear (Viridis)

**Controls:**

- Driver selector
- Lap slider
- Colour-by radio buttons
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Why a track map?**

- Answers Marco's core question: *"Where on the map did we lose time?"*
- Spatial encoding makes patterns **immediately visible** that are hidden in tabular data
- Colour gradient on the track outline is a compact way to overlay one variable on the circuit shape
- **Viridis** for gears (ordinal, sequential), **RdYlGn** for speed (diverging, fast=green)
:::
::::

## Design Decisions Summary {.smaller}

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| **Plotly** instead of Matplotlib | Interactive hover, zoom, pan — essential for telemetry exploration |
| **Dark theme** (#0e1117) | Reduces eye strain during long analysis sessions; matches F1 broadcast aesthetics |
| **Ferrari red** (#e8002d) as primary accent | Immediate brand recognition; Ferrari data stands out from the field |
| **Compound colours** (red/yellow/white) | Leverages established F1 conventions — no learning curve |
| **Background telemetry preloading** | ~30s initial load would frustrate users; thread warms cache on race selection |
| **Distance-based x-axis** (telemetry) | Spatial alignment over time alignment — enables track section comparison |
| **107% median threshold** (outliers) | Standard F1 threshold adapted for outlier filtering to improve readability of charts|
